title: Ex-QB Hasselbeck joins study seeking first living CTE diagnosis
dek: Former NFL quarterback Matt Hasselbeck underwent brain scans, blood tests, and cognitive assessments at Boston University as part of a multi-site NIH-funded research effort to develop a method for diagnosing chronic traumatic encephalopathy in living patients. CTE has been confirmed in over 100 deceased NFL players but cannot yet be identified while patients are alive.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: CTE has been confirmed in more than 100 former NFL players after death, but researchers currently have no way to diagnose the degenerative brain disease in living patients, making baseline studies with volunteers like Hasselbeck critical to developing future treatments.
bottom_line: The research is foundational and early; the small enrollment across all sites means years may pass before a living CTE diagnostic test is ready for clinical use. What would shift the timeline is a breakthrough in protein mapping between CTE and Alzheimer's, or unexpected speed in enrollment and data analysis.
body: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy has been confirmed in more than 100 former NFL players, according to ESPN's reporting, yet doctors cannot diagnose it in a single living patient. That gap is what brought Matt Hasselbeck, the 50-year-old three-time Pro Bowl quarterback, to Boston University for two days of brain scans, blood tests, and cognitive assessments as part of a multi-site research trial aimed at closing it.

Hasselbeck's 17-year NFL career with the Green Bay Packers, Seattle Seahawks, Tennessee Titans, and Indianapolis Colts, spanning 1998 to 2015, gave him a lifetime of head impacts. Before college, he sustained three concussions: one playing football, another on the basketball court, and another while ice skating. He cannot account for the exact number he suffered during his college years at Boston College or his NFL career, partly because locker room culture treated some impacts as routine rather than reportable injuries. Now 50, he is donating his brain for autopsy research after his death and volunteering to help researchers map what living CTE looks like.

The National Institutes of Health awarded $15 million for the study in 2025, per ESPN. The research spans sites in California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida, with more potential locations to follow. The study enrolls two populations: former professional and college football players, and people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease who have never played contact sports and have no history of repetitive head impacts. That control comparison is essential because, according to Michael Alosco, co-director of clinical research at the Boston University CTE Center, many symptoms overlap. CTE can affect brain regions governing behavior and emotion, leading to memory loss, depression, violent mood swings, and cognitive decline, yet researchers note these same symptoms can be attributed to other illnesses.

Alosco said the field has learned a hard lesson: approaches proven effective for Alzheimer's "do not work for CTE." The key to living diagnosis, he explained, lies in mapping protein differences between the two diseases. At the Arizona site, roughly 10 participants have enrolled so far, according to Alosco's colleague Nicholas Ashton, principal investigator in Phoenix. Ashton stated that diagnosing CTE in living patients is "currently mostly guesswork" because symptom overlap with Alzheimer's confounds clinical judgment.

Hasselbeck underwent mental tests, including counting backward from 100 by sevens and reciting the alphabet backward, had blood drawn, received an MRI scan of his brain, and underwent a PET scan that uses a small radioactive tracer to map brain function. Bryan Savage, a 56-year-old former Division III linebacker at Union College in Schenectady, New York, also participated and traveled to Boston for testing. Savage has been diagnosed with depression and ADHD over recent years and found his brain scans appear normal for his age.

High-profile football players including Hall of Famers Junior Seau and Ken Stabler, as well as Aaron Hernandez of the New England Patriots, were all confirmed to have CTE only after death, per ESPN. Alosco expressed cautious optimism: "I'm really hopeful about detecting CTE. I don't think that's too distant. Once we can accurately diagnose, that's when we can start some treatment trials." The study remains in early stages with a small participant pool, and researchers have not yet published a timeline for achieving a conclusive living diagnostic marker.
